papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Correspondence between the layered structure of deep language models and temporal structure of natural language processing in the human brain
papers.research_question: Does the layered hierarchy of deep language models (DLMs) correspond to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain? Specifically, is there a correlation between DLM layer depth and the time at which layers are most predictive of human brain activity?
papers.core_contribution: The layered hierarchy of deep language models (specifically GPT2-XL) corresponds to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain, with early layers predicting early neural responses and later layers predicting later responses in high-order language areas.
papers.conclusion: The internal sequence of computations across layers in deep language models models the temporal hierarchy of language comprehension in the human brain, providing evidence for shared computational principles between DLMs and the brain.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong positive correlation (Pearson r=0.85 in IFG) between DLM layer depth and the time of peak encoding performance in high-order language areas (IFG, TP, aSTG).
Intermediate layers of GPT2-XL (e.g., layer 22 in IFG) provide the best overall prediction of neural activity across language areas, forming an inverted U-shaped curve.
For predictable words, the temporal sequence is clear; for unpredictable words, the pattern is weaker and early layers shift to later lags (around 300ms) in IFG.
The temporal progression timescale increases along the ventral linguistic hierarchy, with the largest within-ROI temporal separation in the Temporal Pole (over 500 ms).
The observed lag-layer correlation is due to nonlinear transformations in the DLM, as linear interpolations between first and last layer embeddings yield significantly lower correlations.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a single DLM (GPT2-XL) and a single narrative stimulus, limiting generalizability.
The temporal resolution of the ECoG measurements, although high, was binned at 50 ms, which may not disambiguate layers that peak at similar times.
The hierarchical structure of DLMs is spatial, while that of the brain is spatiotemporal, representing a fundamental architectural difference.
future_direction: Explore other model architectures (e.g., recurrent, convolutional, or models with explicit temporal dynamics) to see if they better capture brain dynamics.
Use longer contexts and more diverse stimuli to test the robustness of the layer-time correspondence.
Investigate how DLMs might be augmented (e.g., with recurrence or explicit temporal hierarchies) to better model the brain's spatiotemporal language processing.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep language models (DLMs) provide a novel computational paradigm for how the brain processes natural language. Unlike symbolic, rule-based models described in psycholinguistics, DLMs encode words and their context as continuous numerical vectors. These “embeddings” are constructed by a sequence of computations organized in “layers” to ultimately capture surprisingly sophisticated representations of linguistic structures. How does this layered hierarchy map onto the human brain during natural language comprehension? In this study, we used electrocorticography (ECoG) to record neural activity in language areas along the superior temporal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus while human participants listened to a 30-minute spoken narrative. We supplied this same narrative to a high-performing DLM (GPT2-XL) and extracted the contextual embeddings for each word in the story across all 48 layers of the model. We next trained a set of linear encoding models to predict the temporally-evolving neural activity from the embeddings at each layer. We found a striking correspondence between the layer-by-layer sequence of embeddings from GPT2-XL and the temporal sequence of neural activity in language areas. In addition, we found evidence for the gradual accumulation of recurrent information along the linguistic processing hierarchy. However, we also noticed additional neural processes in the brain, but not in DLMs, during the processing of surprising (unpredictable) words. These findings point to a connection between human language processing and DLMs where the layer-by-layer accumulation of contextual information in DLM embeddings matches the temporal dynamics of neural activity in high-order language areas.

papers.title: Neuron Specialization: Leveraging intrinsic task modularity for multilingual machine translation
papers.research_question: How do neurons in multilingual translation models exhibit language-specific modularity, and can this be leveraged to reduce interference and improve translation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that FFN neurons in multilingual models exhibit language-specific modularity, and introduces Neuron Specialization, a method that leverages this to reduce interference and improve translation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that intrinsic modularity in multilingual models can be leveraged to improve translation performance by reducing interference and enhancing transfer, with Neuron Specialization providing consistent gains.
papers.key_findings:
FFN neurons in multilingual translation models activate in a language-specific way, with overlaps indicating linguistic proximity.
The specialization of neurons evolves across layers, becoming more language-agnostic in the encoder and more specific in the decoder.
The proposed Neuron Specialization method, which updates task-specific neurons via sparse networks, consistently improves translation quality over baselines.
This method effectively reduces negative interference in high-resource languages and boosts knowledge transfer in low-resource languages.
Neuron Specialization is efficient, requiring minimal extra parameters and time compared to adapter-based methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to multilingual machine translation and does not explore other multilingual NLP tasks.
Analysis is confined to feed-forward network components, excluding other Transformer elements like attention mechanisms.
Neuron identification relies on ReLU activation states; other activation functions like GELU are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the exploration to a broader range of Multilingual Natural Language Processing tasks beyond translation.
Investigate the modularity of other Transformer components such as attention mechanisms or layer normalization.
Explore neuron specialization for FFNs using activation functions other than ReLU, such as GELU.
papers.abstract: Training a unified multilingual model promotes knowledge transfer but inevitably introduces negative interference. Language-specific modeling methods show promise in reducing interference. However, they often rely on heuristics to distribute capacity and struggle to foster cross-lingual transfer via isolated modules. In this paper, we explore intrinsic task modularity within multilingual networks and leverage these observations to circumvent interference under multilingual translation. We show that neurons in the feed-forward layers tend to be activated in a language-specific manner. Meanwhile, these specialized neurons exhibit structural overlaps that reflect language proximity, which progress across layers. Based on these findings, we propose Neuron Specialization, an approach that identifies specialized neurons to modularize feed-forward layers and then continuously updates them through sparse networks. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves consistent performance gains over strong baselines with additional analyses demonstrating reduced interference and increased knowledge transfer.

papers.title: Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment during LLM Training
papers.research_question: How does cross-lingual alignment emerge during the pre-training of multilingual large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between cross-lingual neuron overlap and zero-shot transfer performance in multilingual LLMs, and reveals non-monotonic alignment dynamics during pre-training with drops in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that shared neurons encoding linguistic features are tightly connected to cross-lingual transfer ability, providing insights into multilingual pretraining dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron overlap for linguistic features increases during pre-training but experiences severe drops in smaller model scales like BLOOM560m and BLOOM1b1.
There is a statistically significant, strong correlation between neuron overlap and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on tasks like POS tagging and XNLI.
Larger models (e.g., BLOOM1b7) show more monotonic growth in alignment, suggesting a scaling law effect.
Drops in alignment correspond to degradation in both in-language and cross-lingual performance.
The emergence of cross-lingual alignment is not steady and can pass through sub-optimal regions during training.
papers.limitation:
Focus on BLOOM checkpoints with large intervals, so findings might not apply to finer-grained training windows.
Only consider autoregressive models with the same objective and training dataset; varying these may result in different patterns.
Focus on alignment of languages seen during pretraining, leaving generalization to unseen languages for future research.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable levels of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance. We speculate that this is predicated on their ability to align languages without explicit supervision from parallel sentences. While representations of translationally equivalent sentences in different languages are known to be similar after convergence, however, it remains unclear how such cross-lingual alignment emerges during pre-training of LLMs. Our study leverages intrinsic probing techniques, which identify which subsets of neurons encode linguistic features, to correlate the degree of cross-lingual neuron overlap with the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for a given model. In particular, we rely on checkpoints of BLOOM, a multilingual autoregressive LLM, across different training steps and model scales. We observe a high correlation between neuron overlap and downstream performance, which supports our hypothesis on the conditions leading to effective cross-lingual transfer. Interestingly, we also detect a degradation of both implicit alignment and multilingual abilities in certain phases of the pre-training process, providing new insights into the multilingual pretraining dynamics.

papers.title: Attribution Analysis of Grammatical Dependencies in LSTMs
papers.research_question: Does the LSTM language model capture grammatical dependencies (subject-verb agreement) by using spurious correlations or by actually matching verbs with their subjects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LSTM language models enforce subject-verb agreement by identifying the subject noun, not by relying on spurious correlations, as demonstrated through layer-wise relevance propagation attribution analysis.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM language model enforces subject-verb agreement in an interpretable manner, and its success on the agreement task is not due to Clever Hans behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model prediction accuracy on subject-verb agreement is positively correlated with its ability to assign higher relevance scores to the subject noun (N1) compared to other nouns (N2).
Determiners (The/the) adjust the magnitude and sometimes direction of the relevance introduced by nouns.
Polysemous verbs (like 'like') can bias the model and cause prediction errors.
For coordinated verb constructions (SVP and LVP), the model uses an alternative strategy that relies on verb coordination rather than solely identifying the subject.
The model fails on object relative clauses (ORC) and likely relies on Clever Hans behavior for that construction.
papers.limitation:
The work does not show that LSTMs can infer stack-like representations of hierarchical syntactic structure or memory-bounded approximations thereof.
The TSE templates are simple in terms of embedding depth and dependency length, limiting the complexity of the syntactic structures evaluated.
future_direction: Exploring whether LSTMs can infer hierarchical syntactic structure and handle more complex syntactic constructions.
papers.abstract: LSTM language models have been shown to capture syntax-sensitive grammatical dependencies such as subject-verb agreement with a high degree of accuracy (Linzen et al., 2016, inter alia). However, questions remain regarding whether they do so using spurious correlations, or whether they are truly able to match verbs with their subjects. This paper argues for the latter hypothesis. Using layer-wise relevance propagation (Bach et al., 2015), a technique that quantifies the contributions of input features to model behavior, we show that LSTM performance on number agreement is directly correlated with the model's ability to distinguish subjects from other nouns. Our results suggest that LSTM language models are able to infer robust representations of syntactic dependencies.

papers.title: Analysing Neural Language Models: Contextual Decomposition Reveals Default Reasoning in Number and Gender Assignment
papers.research_question: How do LSTM language models process syntactic agreement and co-reference resolution, and what information do they rely on for these tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Generalised Contextual Decomposition (GCD), a method to analyze LSTM language models, and reveals that the models rely on a default reasoning effect (singular and masculine as defaults) for number agreement and gender pronoun resolution.
papers.conclusion: GCD is a powerful method for analyzing LSTM language models, revealing a default reasoning effect in number and gender assignment. The method can be extended to other models and improved with better Shapley value approximations.
papers.key_findings:
The model uses a default reasoning effect: singular and masculine are default categories encoded in the model weights.
For number agreement, plural verbs depend strongly on the subject, while singular verbs do not.
For gender pronoun resolution, the model has a male bias encoded in the intercepts, and female pronouns require explicit evidence.
The model correctly resolves referents for unambiguous gender but shows stereotypical biases for gender-neutral job titles.
GCD can accurately attribute contributions of input phrases and model intercepts to predictions.
future_direction: Extending GCD to attention-based models
Improving gate factorisation with better Shapley value approximators
papers.abstract: Extensive research has recently shown that recurrent neural language models are able to process a wide range of grammatical phenomena. How these models are able to perform these remarkable feats so well, however, is still an open question. To gain more insight into what information LSTMs base their decisions on, we propose a generalisation of Contextual Decomposition (GCD). In particular, this setup enables us to accurately distil which part of a prediction stems from semantic heuristics, which part truly emanates from syntactic cues and which part arise from the model biases themselves instead. We investigate this technique on tasks pertaining to syntactic agreement and co-reference resolution and discover that the model strongly relies on a default reasoning effect to perform these tasks.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared representation space while encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features by projecting representations onto orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes in the representation space, enabling efficient extraction for various tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by perplexity comparisons and subspace distances.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means can induce token predictions in different languages.
There are stable language-neutral axes that encode information like token positions and part-of-speech, which are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
Language-sensitive and language-neutral axes are relatively stable across middle layers, with minimal transformation as representations pass through.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures such as spirals and toruses in the representation space.
future_direction: Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically.
Investigate how nonlinear structures like spirals and toruses arise from and interact with the self-attention mechanism.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Probing LLMs for Joint Encoding of Linguistic Categories
papers.research_question: How are linguistically related syntactic categories jointly encoded in LLMs, and do these patterns hold across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence that linguistically related syntactic categories are jointly encoded in LLMs, with similar patterns across languages and between different levels of the linguistic hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs, supporting the idea that models learn hierarchical and shared representations for syntax across languages.
papers.key_findings:
POS tags that are linguistically related are jointly encoded in both monolingual and multilingual models.
Joint encoding patterns are consistent across English, Italian, and Greek in multilingual models.
Information about linguistic categories can be shared across languages, indicating language-agnostic encoding.
There is evidence of joint encoding between POS tags and dependency relations, suggesting information sharing across tasks.
The cross-neutralization method effectively reveals shared representations without tuning the base models.
papers.limitation:
Limited to encoder-only architectures.
Only three languages are examined.
Limited to syntactic tasks (POS tagging and dependency labeling).
Lack of cross-neutralization effects does not necessarily indicate absence of joint encoding.
future_direction: Extend experiments to more languages, particularly low-resource and typologically distant languages.
Include higher-level semantic tasks such as semantic role labeling and coreference resolution.
Explore other model architectures like encoder-decoder or decoder-only models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance on a range of NLP tasks, due to the general-purpose linguistic knowledge acquired during pretraining. Existing model interpretability research (Tenney et al., 2019) suggests that a linguistic hierarchy emerges in the LLM layers, with lower layers better suited to solving syntactic tasks and higher layers employed for semantic processing. Yet, little is known about how encodings of different linguistic phenomena interact within the models and to what extent processing of linguistically-related categories relies on the same, shared model representations. In this paper, we propose a framework for testing the joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs. Focusing on syntax, we find evidence of joint encoding both at the same (related part-of-speech (POS) classes) and different (POS classes and related syntactic dependency relations) levels of linguistic hierarchy. Our cross-lingual experiments show that the same patterns hold across languages in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: A multilabel approach to morphosyntactic probing
papers.research_question: How well does multilingual BERT encode morphosyntactic features across languages, and which features are recognized as shared cross-linguistically?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilabel probing paradigm for morphosyntactic analysis and demonstrates that multilingual BERT encodes many morphosyntactic features extractably, with some features shared cross-linguistically.
papers.conclusion: Multilabel probing is an effective method for analyzing morphosyntactic representations in multilingual language models, revealing that mBERT encodes many features and that some are represented cross-linguistically.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT-6 holds the most morphosyntactic information, with probes achieving micro-averaged F1 scores between 0.83 and 0.97 for seven languages.
Multilingual probes slightly underperform monolingual probes but exhibit better selectivity, suggesting less memorization.
Cross-lingual transfer experiments show that nouns and verbs are well transferred, while adjectives and nominative case are less consistently recognized across languages.
The multilabel paradigm enables fine-grained analysis of feature co-occurrence and agreement patterns, as demonstrated in a case study of Hebrew determiners.
Probe performance varies across languages due to differences in feature sets and training set sizes, making direct comparison difficult.
papers.limitation: The UD corpora used are from narrow domains (e.g., Wikipedia, news, Bible) and may not capture the full range of linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Probe different multilingual language models to compare their morphosyntactic representations.
Explore how global and feature-level probe performance corresponds to downstream task performance.
Conduct more detailed analyses of specific features and their cross-linguistic transfer.
papers.abstract: We propose using a multilabel probing task to assess the morphosyntactic representations of multilingual word embeddings. This tweak on canonical probing makes it easy to explore morphosyntactic representations, both holistically and at the level of individual features (e.g., gender, number, case), and leads more naturally to the study of how language models handle co-occurring features (e.g., agreement phenomena). We demonstrate this task with multilingual BERT Through this simple but robust paradigm, we verify that multilingual BERT renders many morphosyntactic features simultaneously extractable. We further evaluate the probes on six held-out languages: Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slovenian, Tagalog, and Yorb. This zero-shot style of probing has the added benefit of revealing which cross-linguistic properties a language model recognizes as being shared by multiple languages.

papers.title: Explaining a Neural Attention Model for Aspect-Based Sentiment\n Classification Using Diagnostic Classification
papers.research_question: How do the internal layers of the LCR-Rot-hop model encode word-level information such as part of speech, sentiment value, presence of aspect relation, and aspect-related sentiment value for aspect-based sentiment classification?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes diagnostic classifiers to inspect the LCR-Rot-hop model, finding that lower layers (embeddings) encode part-of-speech and sentiment value, while higher layers (context representations) encode aspect relation and aspect-related sentiment value.
papers.conclusion: The context representation determines mostly the presence of a relation with an aspect and the aspect-related sentiment value, while part-of-speech and sentiment value are better detected by the embedding representations.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings are better at predicting part-of-speech and sentiment value than context representations.
Context representations are better at predicting presence of aspect relation and aspect-related sentiment value than embeddings.
Iterating the rotatory attention mechanism does not improve prediction accuracies of diagnostic classifiers.
The model predicts positive opinions more accurately than negative opinions.
Diagnostic classifiers can accurately extract word-level information from internal layers, indicating what information is encoded.
papers.limitation:
The ontology does not contain all relevant words, and the sentiment score from NLTK SentiWordNet might not be correct.
Prediction accuracy is computed over all words, not only sentiment-indicating words, which may affect understanding.
future_direction: Optimise the hyper-parameters of the LCR-Rot-hop model and the diagnostic classifiers.
Better specify the sentiment value and the presence of a relation towards the aspect.
Compute the prediction accuracy only over the words that indicate the sentiment value of the opinion.
papers.abstract:
Many high performance machine learning models for Aspect-Based Sentiment
Classification (ABSC) produce black box models, and therefore barely explain
how they classify a certain sentiment value towards an aspect. In this paper,
we propose explanation models, that inspect the internal dynamics of a
state-of-the-art neural attention model, the LCR-Rot-hop, by using a technique
called Diagnostic Classification. Our diagnostic classifier is a simple neural
network, which evaluates whether the internal layers of the LCR-Rot-hop model
encode useful word information for classification, i.e., the part of speech,
the sentiment value, the presence of aspect relation, and the aspect-related
sentiment value of words. We conclude that the lower layers in the LCR-Rot-hop
model encode the part of speech and the sentiment value, whereas the higher
layers represent the presence of a relation with the aspect and the
aspect-related sentiment value of words.

papers.title: Just-in-time and distributed task representations in language models
papers.research_question: When are transferrable task representations formed in language models during in-context learning, and how do they change over the context?
papers.core_contribution: Transferrable task representations in language models evolve non-monotonically and sporadically, activating only at key tokens, while a persistent representation of task identity is maintained throughout the context.
papers.conclusion: Language models form multiple types of task representations during in-context learning, with transferrable representations activating sporadically and task identity persisting, revealing a complex and nuanced dynamic of the model's internal state.
papers.key_findings:
Transferrable task representations (e.g., task vectors) accrue evidence from multiple in-context examples but form sporadically and non-monotonically.
Task identity representations are robustly decodable from residual activations across most tokens in the context, persisting throughout.
Transferrable task representations exhibit strong temporal locality, forming effectively only at specific tokens (e.g., the colon token before answer generation).
In longer- and mixed-generation tasks, transferrable task representations often decay over output units, showing semantic locality and limited task scope.
For complex tasks requiring state tracking or combining distinct subtasks, effective task representations are more distributed across tokens.
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot recontextualization remains challenging for tasks that require intermediate-state tracking or more complicated computation.
Overriding token activations at intermediate layers with task vectors may cause the model to lose task state information formed in earlier layers.
future_direction: Study the mechanistic bases for the strong temporal and scope locality observed in models' in-context transferrable task representations.
papers.abstract: Many of language models' impressive capabilities originate from their in-context learning: based on instructions or examples, they can infer and perform new tasks without weight updates. In this work, we investigate when representations for new tasks are formed in language models, and how these representations change over the course of context. We study two different task representations: those that are ''transferrable'' -- vector representations that can transfer task contexts to another model instance, even without the full prompt -- and simpler representations of high-level task categories. We show that transferrable task representations evolve in non-monotonic and sporadic ways, while task identity representations persist throughout the context. Specifically, transferrable task representations exhibit a two-fold locality. They successfully condense evidence when more examples are provided in the context. But this evidence accrual process exhibits strong temporal locality along the sequence dimension, coming online only at certain tokens -- despite task identity being reliably decodable throughout the context. In some cases, transferrable task representations also show semantic locality, capturing a small task ''scope'' such as an independent subtask. Language models thus represent new tasks on the fly through both an inert, sustained sensitivity to the task and an active, just-in-time representation to support inference.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Explaining a neural attention model for aspect-based sentiment classification using diagnostic classification
papers.research_question: How does the LCR-Rot-hop model encode useful word information (part of speech, sentiment value, presence of aspect relation, aspect-related sentiment value) in its internal layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses diagnostic classifiers to analyze the LCR-Rot-hop model, finding that lower layers (embeddings, hidden states) encode part-of-speech and sentiment value, while higher layers (context representations) encode presence of aspect relation and aspect-related sentiment value.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers can reveal what information is encoded in different layers of the LCR-Rot-hop model, with lower layers encoding part-of-speech and sentiment value, and higher layers encoding aspect-related information.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings and hidden states are better at predicting part-of-speech and sentiment value.
Context representations are better at predicting presence of aspect relation and aspect-related sentiment value.
The context representations across multiple hops do not show significant variation in predictive performance.
The LCR-Rot-hop model predicts positive opinions more accurately than negative opinions.
Diagnostic classifiers can reveal what information is encoded in different layers of a neural network.
papers.limitation:
The ontology used to determine sentiment and aspect relation does not contain all relevant words, and the sentiment score from NLTK SentiWordNet (based on the most frequent word form) might be incorrect.
The prediction accuracy is computed over all words, not just the sentiment-indicating words, which may obscure the effect of key words on the final classification.
future_direction: Optimize the hyperparameters of the LCR-Rot-hop model and the diagnostic classifiers.
Better specify the sentiment value and the presence of a relation towards the aspect, as the current ontology and SentiWordNet have limitations.
Compute prediction accuracy only over the words that indicate the sentiment value of the opinion to better understand their effect.
Apply the diagnostic classification method to other sentiment datasets beyond restaurant reviews.
papers.abstract: Many high performance machine learning models for Aspect-Based Sentiment Classification (ABSC) produce black box models, and therefore barely explain how they classify a certain sentiment value towards an aspect. In this paper, we propose explanation models, that inspect the internal dynamics of a state-of-the-art neural attention model, the LCR-Rot-hop, by using a technique called Diagnostic Classification. Our diagnostic classifier is a simple neural network, which evaluates whether the internal layers of the LCR-Rot-hop model encode useful word information for classification, i.e., the part of speech, the sentiment value, the presence of aspect relation, and the aspect-related sentiment value of words. We conclude that the lower layers in the LCR-Rot-hop model encode the part of speech and the sentiment value, whereas the higher layers represent the presence of a relation with the aspect and the aspect-related sentiment value of words.

papers.title: Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic Generalization in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the ability of neural language models to make syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure, and how does structural supervision affect learning outcomes and syntactic invariance?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models can learn syntactic generalizations from few examples, and explicit structural supervision improves both few-shot learning and syntactic invariance across transformations.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models are capable of inducing syntactic features from minimal exposure and show some invariance to syntactic transformations, with structural supervision enhancing these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neural models show robust few-shot learning for nominal number and verbal argument structure after minimal exposure.
Structurally supervised models (ActionLSTM and RNNG) outperform the LSTM model in most syntactic generalization tests.
Models demonstrate syntactic invariance by transferring generalizations learned in base contexts to transformed contexts.
There is a singular bias for nouns and a transitive bias for verbs in few-shot learning, with models assuming default categories when evidence is sparse.
Accuracy often improves with increased exposure for some tests, particularly for structurally supervised models.
papers.limitation: The small training data size poses limitations and suggests the need for scaling to larger datasets for better generalization.
future_direction: Scaling the carefully-controlled methods to larger data settings.
papers.abstract: Humans can learn structural properties about a word from minimal experience, and deploy their learned syntactic representations uniformly in different grammatical contexts. We assess the ability of modern neural language models to reproduce this behavior in English and evaluate the effect of structural supervision on learning outcomes. First, we assess few-shot learning capabilities by developing controlled experiments that probe models' syntactic nominal number and verbal argument structure generalizations for tokens seen as few as two times during training. Second, we assess invariance properties of learned representation: the ability of a model to transfer syntactic generalizations from a base context (e.g., a simple declarative active-voice sentence) to a transformed context (e.g., an interrogative sentence). We test four models trained on the same dataset: an n-gram baseline, an LSTM, and two LSTM-variants trained with explicit structural supervision (Dyer et al.,2016; Charniak et al., 2016). We find that in most cases, the neural models are able to induce the proper syntactic generalizations after minimal exposure, often from just two examples during training, and that the two structurally supervised models generalize more accurately than the LSTM model. All neural models are able to leverage information learned in base contexts to drive expectations in transformed contexts, indicating that they have learned some invariance properties of syntax.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Large LSTMs trained on large datasets can represent syntactic state comparably to an explicitly syntactic model (RNNG), and data size is crucial for learning fine-grained lexical cues to syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: All models show basic incremental syntactic state representation, but capturing fine-grained lexical cues requires large amounts of data, while coarse-grained structure can be learned with either syntactic supervision or large data.
papers.key_findings:
All tested models show basic evidence of incremental syntactic state representation (e.g., subordinate clause licensing).
Only the large LSTMs (GRNN, JRNN) and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty).
All models show NP/Z garden path effects, but only large LSTMs are sensitive to verb transitivity as a cue.
All models show MV/RR garden path effects, but only large LSTMs and the RNNG are sensitive to verb morphology as a cue.
The representation of syntactic state degrades with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM).
future_direction: Using psycholinguistic methodology as a basis for more systematic tests of the linguistic competence of NLP systems.
papers.abstract: We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset; and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: Influence Paths for Characterizing Subject-Verb Number Agreement in LSTM Language Models
papers.research_question: Does an LSTM language model learn structural features of natural languages such as subject-verb number agreement, and how does it handle this concept?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces influence paths, a method to decompose the influence of a concept (e.g., subject number) on an output (e.g., verb number) into paths across gates and neurons of an LSTM, showing that subject-verb agreement is concentrated in a primary path and specific neurons.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM language model handles subject-verb number agreement in a general and localized manner, with a primary path and specific neurons responsible, and errors arise from competing influences rather than lack of structural capability.
papers.key_findings:
The same primary path carries the largest positive attribution for subject-verb number agreement across all contexts.
Two specific neurons (125 and 337 in the second layer) are consistently the most influential for number agreement.
Attractors (intervening nouns of opposite number) contribute negative attribution along the same primary path, while helpful nouns contribute positive attribution.
Model compression experiments show that the primary path accounts for most of the subject number agreement concept.
The primary path remains dominant even in the presence of attractors, indicating that errors are due to attractor influence rather than lack of concept.
papers.limitation: The analysis is based on datasets with limited context size, and the number of paths grows exponentially with context size, which may limit scalability to longer contexts.
future_direction: Investigate longer contexts and the diminishing dominance of the primary path.
Expand the method to more complicated sentences with clausal structures or other syntactic/semantic signals like coreference or gender agreement.
papers.abstract: LSTM-based recurrent neural networks are the state-of-the-art for many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Despite their performance, it is unclear whether, or how, LSTMs learn structural features of natural languages such as subject-verb number agreement in English. Lacking this understanding, the generality of LSTM performance on this task and their suitability for related tasks remains uncertain. Further, errors cannot be properly attributed to a lack of structural capability, training data omissions, or other exceptional faults. We introduce *influence paths*, a causal account of structural properties as carried by paths across gates and neurons of a recurrent neural network. The approach refines the notion of influence (the subject's grammatical number has influence on the grammatical number of the subsequent verb) into a set of gate or neuron-level paths. The set localizes and segments the concept (e.g., subject-verb agreement), its constituent elements (e.g., the subject), and related or interfering elements (e.g., attractors). We exemplify the methodology on a widely-studied multi-layer LSTM language model, demonstrating its accounting for subject-verb number agreement. The results offer both a finer and a more complete view of an LSTM's handling of this structural aspect of the English language than prior results based on diagnostic classifiers and ablation.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: The emergence of number and syntax units in LSTM language models
papers.research_question: How do LSTMs capture syntax-sensitive generalizations such as long-distance number agreement, and do they rely on heuristics or genuine syntactic processing mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that long-distance number agreement in LSTMs is managed by specialized 'number units' and a 'syntax unit', providing direct evidence that LSTMs learn genuine syntactic processing mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: LSTMs trained on unannotated corpus data learn to perform structure-dependent linguistic operations, suggesting that raw linguistic input and generic memory mechanisms may suffice to induce non-trivial grammatical rules.
papers.key_findings:
Two 'number units' (singular and plural) encode and store grammatical number information across long-range dependencies.
A 'syntax unit' encodes the main subject-verb dependency and controls the gates of the number units via strong afferent connections.
Number is also encoded in a distributed manner by short-range units, but these are not syntax-sensitive and are affected by intervening nouns.
The interaction between syntax and number units suggests that LSTMs learn structure-based syntactic representations, not just superficial heuristics.
The study provides a mechanistic understanding of how LSTMs perform long-distance number agreement at the single neuron level.
papers.limitation:
The study excludes agreement across relative clauses, which adds complexity.
The analysis is limited to a single LSTM model and English, and may not generalize to other architectures, languages, or domains.
future_direction: Explore how the encoding pattern varies across network architectures, hyperparameters, languages, and domains.
Investigate the timecourse of emergence of the found behaviour over training time.
Test predictions on human brain dynamics to see if similar distinctions between short-range and long-range units exist.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that LSTMs trained on a generic language modeling objective capture syntax-sensitive generalizations such as long-distance number agreement. We have however no mechanistic understanding of how they accomplish this remarkable feat. Some have conjectured it depends on heuristics that do not truly take hierarchical structure into account. We present here a detailed study of the inner mechanics of number tracking in LSTMs at the single neuron level. We discover that long-distance number information is largely managed by two `number units'. Importantly, the behaviour of these units is partially controlled by other units independently shown to track syntactic structure. We conclude that LSTMs are, to some extent, implementing genuinely syntactic processing mechanisms, paving the way to a more general understanding of grammatical encoding in LSTMs.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
Intervening on these temporal difference features (lesioning or clamping) impairs performance and reduces correlations, demonstrating their causal involvement.
In a grid world task, Llama uses temporal difference-like features to predict the actions of a Q-learning agent.
In a graph learning task, Llama learns global graph structure similarly to the successor representation, and temporal difference features support this learning.
papers.limitation:
The sparse autoencoders are task-specific and not suitable for identifying reinforcement learning variables for arbitrary tasks.
A circuit-level understanding of how these representations come about remains unclear.
The alignment between the model's behavior and the Q-learning agent is not perfect.
future_direction: Build more generic sparse autoencoders for arbitrary tasks.
Replicate findings with different large language models.
Achieve a circuit-level understanding of how temporal difference representations are computed.
Extend the Q-learning model to account for repetition tendencies.
papers.abstract: In-context learning, the ability to adapt based on a few examples in the input prompt, is a ubiquitous feature of large language models (LLMs). However, as LLMs' in-context learning abilities continue to improve, understanding this phenomenon mechanistically becomes increasingly important. In particular, it is not well-understood how LLMs learn to solve specific classes of problems, such as reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in-context. Through three different tasks, we first show that Llama $3$ $70$B can solve simple RL problems in-context. We then analyze the residual stream of Llama using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and find representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token. We verify that these representations are indeed causally involved in the computation of TD errors and $Q$-values by performing carefully designed interventions on them. Taken together, our work establishes a methodology for studying and manipulating in-context learning with SAEs, paving the way for a more mechanistic understanding.

papers.title: Are Structural Concepts Universal in Transformer Language Models? Towards Interpretable Cross-Lingual Generalization
papers.research_question: Can explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages enhance cross-lingual generalization in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) are implicitly alignable across languages in transformer LMs, and proposes a meta-learning method to explicitly align these concepts, improving zero-shot and few-shot cross-lingual generalization without updating the LM parameters.
papers.conclusion: Explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages via meta-learning improves cross-lingual generalization, achieving competitive performance and narrowing the gap between languages, particularly for low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
Structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) can be identified based on prototypes in a relatively low-dimensional space of LM representations.
These structural concepts are highly alignable across languages in both encoder-only (mBERT) and decoder-only (LLaMA) models, as measured by RSA and Procrustes analysis.
A meta-learning-based method to align conceptual spaces achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods on syntactic analysis tasks, especially benefiting low-resource languages.
The method reduces the performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages.
The approach provides insights into cross-lingual in-context learning and can be integrated with prompting to improve generalization.
papers.limitation: Variations in alignability between language pairs may stem from insufficient UD treebank data for approximating prototypes and degenerate representation spaces for certain languages due to inadequate pretraining data or tokenization deficiencies.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to other aspects of language to better accommodate linguistic diversity using self-supervised knowledge.
Exploring more expressive probing models to extract structural concepts, especially grammatical relations, from models like LLaMA.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited considerable cross-lingual generalization abilities, whereby they implicitly transfer knowledge across languages. However, the transfer is not equally successful for all languages, especially for low-resource ones, which poses an ongoing challenge. It is unclear whether we have reached the limits of implicit cross-lingual generalization and if explicit knowledge transfer is viable. In this paper, we investigate the potential for explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages to enhance cross-lingual generalization. Using the syntactic aspect of language as a testbed, our analyses of 43 languages reveal a high degree of alignability among the spaces of structural concepts within each language for both encoder-only and decoder-only LLMs. We then propose a meta-learning-based method to learn to align conceptual spaces of different languages, which facilitates zero-shot and few-shot generalization in concept classification and also offers insights into the cross-lingual in-context learning phenomenon. Experiments on syntactic analysis tasks show that our approach achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods and narrows the performance gap between languages, particularly benefiting those with limited resources.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Neural Networks Can Learn Patterns of Island-insensitivity in Norwegian
papers.research_question: Whether Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can learn the distribution of acceptable filler-gap dependencies and cross-linguistic differences in island constraints in Norwegian from input data.
papers.core_contribution: LSTM RNNs can learn cross-linguistic differences in island constraints (e.g., that embedded questions are not islands in Norwegian but subject and adjunct phrases are), supporting the claim that such constraints can be induced from input patterns without domain-specific learning biases.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that RNNs can learn cross-linguistic differences in island constraints from input, leading to a reassessment of the importance of domain-specific learning biases in acquiring such constraints.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM RNNs learn that filler-gap dependencies (FGDs) are unbounded in Norwegian.
LSTM RNNs show reduced filler effects inside subject islands in Norwegian, indicating sensitivity to this constraint.
LSTM RNNs show reduced filler effects inside temporal adjunct islands in Norwegian.
LSTM RNNs treat embedded questions similarly to declarative complements in Norwegian, suggesting they are not islands.
LSTM RNNs exhibit different patterns for whether-islands in English and Norwegian, indicating learning from language-specific input.
papers.limitation:
In Experiment 4, filled gap effects were not robust in subject position, which might be due to that-trace effects or low frequency of embedded subject gaps in training data.
The models might not fully treat adjuncts as islands, as filler effects were not zero in the adjunct island condition.
It is unknown whether the model's active gap-filling behavior mirrors human behavior for Norwegian.
It cannot be verified whether the models learned from direct evidence of FGDs into embedded questions or indirectly.
future_direction: Future work should test the alignment between the model’s performance and human behavior.
Future work using this paradigm should consider the dissociation between filled gap effects and unlicensed gap effects when interpreting results.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can capture abstract generalizations about filler-gap dependencies (FGDs) in English and so-called island constraints on their distribution (Wilcox et al., 2018; 2021). These results have been interpreted as evidence that it is possible, in principle, to induce complex syntactic knowledge from the input without domain-specific learning biases. However, the English results alone do not establish that island constraints were induced from distributional properties of the training data instead of simply reflecting architectural limitations independent of the input to the models. We address this concern by investigating whether such models can learn the distribution of acceptable FGDs in Norwegian, a language that is sensitive to fewer islands than English (Christensen, 1982). Results from five experiments show that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) RNNs can (i) learn that Norwegian FGD formation is unbounded, (ii) recover the island status of temporal adjunct and subject islands, and (iii) learn that Norwegian, unlike English, permits FGDs into two types of embedded questions. The fact that LSTM RNNs can learn cross-linguistic differences in island facts therefore strengthens the claim that RNN language models can induce the constraints from patterns in the input.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small.
